title: Corona Says
html:
"Corona Says" is a short poem written by the Nepali writer Vishnu S. Rai during the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020. Its trick is simple and powerful: the virus itself is given a voice. Instead of a human complaining about a disease, a disease complains about human beings. By the end of the poem the reader is no longer sure which of the two is the real infection of the earth.

What the exam wants from this poem

Examiners ask three things again and again: who is the speaker (the coronavirus, not the poet), what charges the speaker brings against humankind, and why the poem is called a satire. Learn the list of human crimes the virus names, and learn to say in one sentence that the poem turns the accusation around — the accused becomes the accuser.

8.1 About the poet

Vishnu S. Rai is a contemporary Nepali writer, translator and linguist who writes in both Nepali and English. For many years he taught English Education at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, and he has been an active figure in NELTA (the Nepal English Language Teachers' Association), for whose journal he has written and edited. His published work spans several kinds of writing: poems and short stories in English, translations between Nepali and English, and academic books on language, linguistics and English language teaching. He is also known as a collector and reteller of Nepali folk material.

Rai does not belong to a formal literary "movement". He is best placed in the generation of Nepali writers who, from the late twentieth century onwards, chose to write creatively in English about Nepali and global subjects, so that Nepali experience could reach readers beyond South Asia. His manner is plain, ironic and conversational — everyday words, short lines, no ornament — and his subjects are usually social: power, hypocrisy, and the gap between what people say and what they do. "Corona Says" is a pandemic poem, written while the whole world was shut indoors in 2020, and it belongs to the large body of literature that the pandemic produced almost overnight.

8.2 Summary

The poem is a dramatic monologue: one speaker talks, and we understand the silent listener only from what the speaker says. The speaker is the coronavirus. The listener is the whole human race. The poem moves through four clear stages, which are best studied one at a time.

Movement 1 — The virus admits it is hated

The virus begins by acknowledging what human beings feel about it. It knows that people hate it, fear it and want it dead, and that they call it a killer. It does not argue with this. It accepts, calmly, that it has caused death and that the world is frightened of it. This quiet, reasonable opening is important: the speaker sounds not like a monster but like someone willing to discuss the charge.

Movement 2 — The virus turns the accusation round

Having accepted the charge, the virus asks who the greater killer really is. It reminds human beings of what they have done to the earth long before any virus arrived: forests cut down, rivers and air poisoned, other living creatures hunted, caged and killed for pleasure or profit, and wars in which human beings destroyed their own kind in millions. The point the virus makes is one of proportion. Whatever harm a virus has done in a few months, humankind has done far more, for far longer, and on purpose. A virus kills because that is its nature; people destroy while knowing exactly what they are doing.

Movement 3 — The virus as a teacher of equality

The virus then describes its own most uncomfortable quality: it makes no distinctions. It does not ask whether a body is rich or poor, powerful or powerless, of one religion or another, of one colour or another, from a rich country or a poor one. Money, weapons, armies and titles are of no use against it. In a world organised around exactly such differences, this is presented as a kind of grim lesson: the virus has shown human beings the equality they preach but never practise.

Movement 4 — The earth breathes, and the warning

Finally the virus points to what happened while human beings stayed shut in their houses. Factories and vehicles stopped; the air cleared; rivers ran cleaner; birds and animals were heard and seen in places from which people had driven them away. The planet, in other words, recovered a little the moment human activity paused — which quietly proves the virus's case about who the real destroyer is. The poem closes on a conditional note rather than a triumphant one: the virus will pass, as such things do, but whether human beings have actually learnt anything is left as an open question addressed to the reader.

8.3 Themes

Human destruction of nature. This is the poem's central subject. The virus's list of human crimes is all environmental: trees, water, air, animals. The poem argues that the pandemic is not an accident that fell on an innocent world but a symptom of the way human beings have been treating the planet.

Who is the real killer? The poem is built on a reversal. We open the poem sure that the virus is the villain, and close it wondering about ourselves. The question is left with the reader deliberately.

Death as the great equaliser. The virus is indifferent to wealth, caste, colour, religion and nationality. For a world in which those differences decide everything, this indifference is frightening — and instructive.

Human arrogance. People believed that money, science, armies and borders made them masters of the earth. A microscopic organism that cannot even be seen showed how thin that mastery was.

Nature's power to heal itself. The clearing skies and returning birds of 2020 show that the damage is not yet beyond repair, provided human pressure is reduced. This is the one hopeful note in the poem.

Satire and self-examination. The poem does not preach directly. It hands the microphone to the enemy and lets the enemy's calm voice do the accusing, which makes the criticism much harder to shrug off.

8.4 Form, structure and rhyme

Form. "Corona Says" is written in free verse — verse with no fixed metre and no rhyme scheme. The lines are short and of unequal length, and they break where a speaking voice would pause, not where a metrical pattern would end. If you are asked for the rhyme scheme, the correct answer is that the poem has none: there is no ABAB or AABB pattern to write out, because the poet has deliberately given it up.

Why free verse suits this poem. A regular metre would make the virus sound like a song or a hymn. Free verse makes it sound like someone talking to you across a table — patient, matter-of-fact, unhurried. The plainness is the point. The poet also avoids grand poetic vocabulary, so that the horror in the content (forests, wars, dead bodies) is left to speak for itself.

Structure. The poem is a dramatic monologue, and its structure is the structure of an argument, not of a story: charge accepted, counter-charge made, evidence given, conclusion left open. The "you" addressed throughout is the reader, which is what gives the poem its uncomfortable force — we are not watching an accusation, we are receiving one.

Voice and device. Giving speech, reasoning and feeling to a virus is personification used as the frame of the whole poem, not as a decoration in one line. Everything else in the poem depends on it.

A very common mistake

Do not write that "the poet says he hates human beings" or that "the poet describes the coronavirus". Neither is true. The poet does not speak at all. The speaker is the virus, and the poet's opinion reaches us only indirectly, through what he makes the virus say. Confusing poet with speaker loses marks in almost every literature paper.

8.5 Poetic devices

Because the poem is modern and in copyright, the table below names each device and the place in the poem where it works, rather than reprinting the lines.

Device Where it appears Effect
Personification the virus speaks as "I" and reasons like a person Makes the whole poem possible; an enemy is allowed to state its case
Apostrophe (direct address) the repeated "you" aimed at humankind The reader is put in the dock; the criticism becomes personal
Irony a killer disease lecturing us on killing Exposes human hypocrisy far better than direct preaching
Metaphor humankind pictured as the true disease of the earth Reverses villain and victim in a single stroke
Imagery (visual) cleared skies, clean rivers, animals moving freely in empty streets Turns an argument into something the reader can see
Imagery (of violence) felled forests, poisoned water, caged and slaughtered animals, war dead Piles up evidence so that the counter-charge feels proved
Symbolism the virus stands for nature's revenge and for a warning Lifts the poem above one disease in one year
Hyperbole the sweeping claim that human beings have destroyed everything they touch The exaggeration is emotional, not factual; it conveys anger
Repetition / anaphora the clauses of accusation stacked one on another Creates the rhythm of a courtroom charge-sheet
Enjambment the short lines running on without punctuation Keeps the speaking voice moving and refuses a singsong effect
Alliteration the poem's clusters of repeated opening consonants Small musical touches inside an otherwise plain style
Satire the poem as a whole Uses ridicule of human behaviour to demand a change in it

8.6 Glossary

Word Meaning
corona crown; the coronavirus is so named because of the crown-like spikes on its surface
pandemic a disease outbreak spread over many countries at the same time
epidemic a disease outbreak confined to one area or population
virus a microscopic agent that can reproduce only inside the living cells of another organism
monologue a long speech by one person
dramatic monologue a poem in which an invented speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener
free verse poetry without regular metre or rhyme
personification giving human qualities, speech or feeling to a thing, animal or idea
apostrophe a direct address to an absent person, a group, or an abstract thing
satire writing that attacks folly or wrongdoing through ridicule
irony a gap between what is said or expected and what is actually the case
hypocrisy claiming to hold standards that one's own behaviour does not follow
lockdown an official order confining people to their homes
quarantine keeping a person apart from others to stop infection spreading
deforestation the clearing away of forests
pollution the poisoning of air, water or land by harmful substances
equaliser something that removes differences of rank or wealth
arrogance an exaggerated sense of one's own importance or power
indifferent showing no preference or concern either way
revenge harm done in return for harm received

Chapter summary

  • "Corona Says" by Vishnu S. Rai is a dramatic monologue in free verse in which the coronavirus speaks to the whole human race.
  • Its four movements are: the virus accepts that it is hated; it accuses human beings of far greater destruction; it points out that it alone treats all people equally; and it shows that nature began to heal the moment people stopped.
  • Central themes: destruction of the environment, human arrogance and hypocrisy, death as an equaliser, nature's capacity to recover, and the reversal of villain and victim.
  • There is no rhyme scheme and no metre — the plain speaking voice of free verse is chosen on purpose.
  • The governing device is personification; the governing mode is satire; the governing effect is irony.
  • The poet never speaks in his own voice. Never confuse the poet with the speaker.

Practice questions

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. Who is the speaker in "Corona Says", and who is being addressed? [2]
  2. What charges does the virus bring against human beings? [2]
  3. In what sense is the coronavirus called an equaliser in the poem? [2]
  4. What changes in nature does the speaker point to as evidence for its argument? [2]
  5. Why has the poet chosen free verse instead of a regular metre? [2]
  6. What is a dramatic monologue? Show how "Corona Says" fits the definition. [2]
  7. Explain the irony on which the poem depends. [2]
Model answers — short questions

1. The speaker is the coronavirus itself, given a human voice by the poet. It addresses the whole human race — the repeated "you" of the poem. The poet himself never speaks directly; his opinion reaches us only through what the virus says.

2. The virus accuses human beings of cutting down forests, poisoning rivers and the air, hunting, caging and killing other creatures, and destroying millions of their own kind in wars. Its point is that all this damage was deliberate, long-lasting and far greater than the harm a virus can do.

3. The virus does not ask whether the body it enters is rich or poor, of which country, colour, caste or religion, or how powerful its owner is. Wealth, weapons and rank give no protection. In a world divided by exactly these differences, the virus treats everybody the same, and so becomes an equaliser.

4. During the lockdown the air became clear, the rivers ran cleaner, and birds and wild animals reappeared in places from which people had driven them. The earth recovered as soon as human activity stopped, which supports the virus's claim that human beings, not viruses, are the planet's real problem.

5. Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme, so the poem sounds like ordinary speech rather than a song. That plain, calm, conversational voice makes the virus's accusation sound reasonable, and keeps the reader's attention on the terrible content instead of on pretty sound patterns.

6. A dramatic monologue is a poem in which an invented speaker, who is not the poet, talks at length to a silent listener whose presence we infer from the speech. In "Corona Says" the invented speaker is the virus, the silent listener is humankind, and we learn what humankind feels ("you hate me") only from the virus's words.

7. The irony is that a deadly disease takes the moral high ground and lectures human beings about killing. The accused becomes the accuser, and the creature we call a killer proves that we kill more. The gap between our view of ourselves as civilised and the evidence the virus produces is the poem's irony.

Long answer questions (5 marks each)

  1. "Corona Says" reverses the roles of villain and victim. Discuss. [5]
  2. Discuss "Corona Says" as a satire on modern human civilisation. [5]
  3. Examine the form and language of "Corona Says" and show how they serve its meaning. [5]
Model answers — long questions

1. The poem begins where the reader already stands: the virus is the killer, human beings are its victims, and the speaker openly admits that it is hated and wished dead. Having accepted that charge, it immediately reverses it. It asks who has done more killing, and answers with a list of human acts — forests cut down, rivers and air poisoned, animals hunted and caged, wars in which millions of human beings destroyed one another. The comparison is one of scale and of intention: a virus spreads because that is its nature, while people destroy knowing exactly what they do. The reversal is then confirmed by evidence from the lockdown. When human activity stopped, the sky cleared, the water cleaned itself and animals returned to the streets — so the planet was healthier without us than with us. By the end, the word "virus" has changed owners: the true infection of the earth is humankind, and the disease is merely a symptom. Because the accusation comes from the enemy's own mouth and not from the poet's, the reader cannot dismiss it as preaching, and has to sit with the discomfort.

2. Satire attacks human folly and wrongdoing by holding it up to ridicule, and that is precisely what this poem does. Its satirical method is to give the speech to the coronavirus, so that human behaviour is described from outside by somebody with no reason to flatter us. The targets are exact. First, our hypocrisy: we call the virus a murderer while conducting wars and slaughtering other species. Second, our arrogance: we believed money, technology, armies and borders had made us masters of the earth, and an organism too small to see undid that belief in weeks. Third, our inequality: we announce that all human beings are equal and then organise the world by wealth, colour, religion and nationality, and it takes a disease — which asks none of those questions — to treat us all alike. Fourth, our carelessness towards nature, proved by how quickly the earth improved without us. The tone is not shrill; the virus is calm, patient and almost polite, and this restraint sharpens the attack. The poem ends not with a punishment but with a question about whether we have learnt anything, which is satire's real aim: not to wound but to correct.

3. The poem is written in free verse: the lines are short, of unequal length, and there is no metre and no rhyme scheme at all. This is a deliberate choice. A regular pattern would have made the virus sound like a chant or a hymn, whereas free verse makes it sound like a person speaking quietly and reasonably to someone across a table, which is far more unsettling. The vocabulary matches the form: ordinary, unornamented words, so that the frightening content — felled forests, poisoned water, war dead — is allowed to do the work without help from grand poetic language. Structurally the poem is an argument rather than a story: the charge is accepted, a counter-charge is made, evidence is produced, and the conclusion is handed to the reader. Two devices hold everything together. Personification frames the whole poem, since without a speaking virus there is no poem at all. Apostrophe — the insistent "you" — keeps the reader inside the poem as the accused rather than outside it as an observer. Enjambment lets the short lines run on so the voice never falls into singsong, and the stacked clauses of accusation give the passage the rhythm of a charge-sheet being read out in court. Form, language and meaning are therefore inseparable: a poem about stripping away human pretence is itself stripped of poetic decoration.

Reference to the context

  1. The speaker tells human beings that it does not ask whether a body belongs to a rich person or a poor one, to one religion or another, before it enters.(a) Who is the speaker?(b) What quality of the speaker is being described here?(c) What comment on human society does this make? [5]
  2. The speaker points out that while people remained shut inside their houses, the sky grew clear, the rivers ran clean, and the birds and animals came back.(a) Which period is being described?(b) Why does the speaker mention these changes?(c) What does the passage suggest about the relation between human beings and nature? [5]
Model answers — reference to the context

1. (a) The speaker is the coronavirus, which the poet has personified and allowed to address humankind throughout the poem. (b) It describes the virus's complete indifference to human distinctions. It infects anyone, and wealth, power, caste, colour, nationality and religion give no protection. This is why the poem presents it as the one true equaliser. (c) The comment is a bitter one about human hypocrisy. Human society claims that all people are equal, yet it is organised by exactly the differences the virus ignores. It has taken a disease to give human beings the equality their own declarations promise but their behaviour denies. The lines therefore work as satire: the virus is not boasting, it is exposing us.

2. (a) The passage describes the COVID-19 lockdown of 2020, when factories, vehicles and daily movement stopped almost everywhere in the world. (b) The speaker mentions these changes as evidence in its argument. Having claimed that human beings, not viruses, are the earth's real destroyers, it points to what happened the moment human activity paused: the proof of the claim is that the planet immediately began to recover. (c) The passage suggests that the relationship has become one-sided and harmful — nature does not need human beings, but suffers from them, and is able to heal itself quickly if the pressure is lifted. It carries one hopeful implication: the damage is not yet beyond repair. Whether people will choose to reduce that pressure after the pandemic is the open question on which the poem ends.
